classification.difficultyReason: Both methods are prescribed; choose familiar angles for the difference expansion and take the positive half-angle square root to equate two expressions for the same cosine.

content.prompt:
By using $\cos 2\theta=2\cos^2\theta-1$ and a difference expansion to find $\cos15^\circ$, show that
$$\frac{\sqrt{2+\sqrt3}}2=\frac{\sqrt6+\sqrt2}4.$$

answer.short:
$$\cos15^\circ=\frac{\sqrt{2+\sqrt3}}2=\frac{\sqrt6+\sqrt2}4.$$

Use the cosine double-angle formula and expand $\cos(45^\circ-30^\circ)$.
answer.worked:
Using the double-angle formula:
$$\begin{align*}\cos30^\circ&=2\cos^2 15^\circ-1\\\cos^2 15^\circ&=\frac{1+\cos30^\circ}{2}\\\cos^2 15^\circ&=\frac{2+\sqrt3}{4}\\\cos15^\circ&=\frac{\sqrt{2+\sqrt3}}2.\end{align*}$$
The positive square root is used because $15^\circ$ is acute.

Using a difference expansion:
$$\begin{align*}\cos15^\circ&=\cos(45^\circ-30^\circ)\\\cos15^\circ&=\cos45^\circ\cos30^\circ+\sin45^\circ\sin30^\circ\\\cos15^\circ&=\frac{\sqrt2}{2}\cdot\frac{\sqrt3}{2}+\frac{\sqrt2}{2}\cdot\frac12\\\cos15^\circ&=\frac{\sqrt6+\sqrt2}{4}.\end{align*}$$
Both expressions equal $\cos15^\circ$, so
$$\frac{\sqrt{2+\sqrt3}}2=\frac{\sqrt6+\sqrt2}4.$$
